opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. The core motivation behind PixelRush was a gap we kept seeing between what diffusion models can do and what people can actually run on their phones. Most text-to-image models are trained at fairly modest resolutions, around 512 or 1024 pixels, but phone displays and cameras work at much higher resolutions. When you push these models beyond their training resolution, you get familiar artifacts: repeated objects, duplicated faces, broken structure, textures that don't hold together.

The usual fixes are either retraining or fine-tuning at high resolution, which is very expensive, or training-free approaches. The training-free methods tend to work in stages: generate at low resolution, upsample, then refine through many denoising steps, often on overlapping patches. Quality can be good, but these pipelines are slow. They can take minutes on a high-end GPU, which rules them out for a smartphone.

So the question we asked was whether we could get high-resolution, structurally coherent images from an existing pretrained model, without retraining, and do it fast enough to be practical on a mobile device.

The main insight was that you don't need to run the full denoising trajectory again at high resolution. The low-resolution pass already sets the global layout and semantics. The high-resolution stage only needs to add fine detail. So we start that stage partway through the process, work patch by patch to keep memory manageable, and blend the patches carefully so you don't see seams. We also made it compatible with few-step, distilled models, so the whole thing needs only a handful of steps.

Taken together, those choices bring the cost down by a large factor compared with earlier tuning-free methods while keeping quality competitive. That makes on-device high-resolution generation realistic rather than just a demo. It matters for latency, and it also matters for privacy, because your prompts and images never have to leave the phone.

r001.rationale: The response mentions patching to keep memory manageable, but does not explain that higher resolution increases memory needs because latent features must be retained during generation.

r002.rationale: It contrasts upsample-and-refine pipelines with PixelRush’s high-resolution stage adding fine detail, conveying that the goal goes beyond merely enlarging an image.

r003.rationale: It says PixelRush aims to produce high-resolution images from an existing pretrained model without retraining it.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The motivation was pretty simple: people want to generate large, detailed images on their phone, and the diffusion models that produce those images were built for the data center. If you take a model like Stable Diffusion and ask it to produce, say, a 2K or 4K image, the compute and memory grow roughly quadratically with resolution because of the attention layers, and the number of denoising steps you need stays high. On a mobile NPU with a strict power and memory budget, that just doesn't work. You either wait minutes, or the device overheats, or it simply runs out of memory.

So with PixelRush we asked: what would it take to make high-resolution generation genuinely interactive on a phone, meaning a few seconds rather than a few minutes, without giving up quality? We approached it from a few directions at once. One was reducing the number of sampling steps through distillation, so the model can get to a good image in a handful of steps instead of twenty or fifty. Another was being smarter about where we spend compute spatially. A lot of a high-resolution image is relatively smooth, and the fine detail is concentrated in certain regions, so we generate a coarse structure at low resolution and then progressively refine, allocating more work only where it matters. And the third was the systems side: quantization, fitting the model into the on-device memory, and mapping the operations so they actually run efficiently on the hardware rather than on paper.

The broader goal, really, was to show that high-resolution generative models don't have to live in the cloud. There are latency reasons for that, there are cost reasons, and increasingly there are privacy reasons. If you can do it on the device you have in your hand, that opens up a very different set of applications, from photo editing to creative tools, where the user expects an immediate response.

r001.rationale: It says memory use grows with resolution because of attention layers, but does not explain that latent features must be retained during generation.

r002.rationale: It describes generating detailed images through coarse-to-fine refinement, but does not distinguish that from simply upsampling an image.

r003.rationale: It describes distillation, refinement, and systems changes, but does not state that PixelRush raises output resolution without substantially modifying existing models.

astra-6.text: The goal with PixelRush was to make high-resolution image generation practical on a smartphone. That means thinking beyond image quality alone: you also have to consider latency, memory, and power consumption. We wanted a user to be able to describe an image and generate it directly on the device, with good visual quality and a short wait, within the constraints of mobile hardware.

r001.rationale: It mentions memory as a mobile constraint, but does not explain that higher-resolution diffusion requires retaining latent features and therefore increases memory use.

r002.rationale: It mentions good visual quality, but does not distinguish generating genuine image detail from simply upsampling.

r003.rationale: It does not say PixelRush would increase the output resolution of existing image-generation models while leaving those models substantially unmodified.

sol-6.1.text: With PixelRush, we wanted to make high-resolution image generation practical on a smartphone. The challenge is that generating a large image requires a lot of computation and memory, and on a phone you also have power and thermal constraints. So the goal was to preserve image quality and detail while reducing that computational burden enough to run on the device. It’s really about bringing that creative capability directly to the user without having to send every request to the cloud.

r001.rationale: It mentions memory demands generally, but does not explain that higher-resolution diffusion requires retaining latent features during generation.

r002.rationale: It says the goal was to preserve quality and detail, but does not distinguish generating genuine detail from simply upsampling.

r003.rationale: It does not state that PixelRush increases the output resolution of existing models or does so without substantially modifying them.
